targets: Posterior septal branches of sphenopalatine artery
title: Epistaxis: anterior and posterior
text:
Little's area (Kiesselbach plexus) on the anterior nasal septum is where septal branches of the sphenopalatine, anterior ethmoidal, greater palatine and superior labial arteries anastomose; about 90% of nosebleeds arise here, from nose picking, dry air, colds or anticoagulants. First aid is to sit forward with the mouth open and firmly pinch the soft part of the nose (not the bridge) for 10 to 20 minutes; persistent anterior bleeding is treated with silver nitrate cautery (one side of the septum at a time, to avoid perforation) or nasal packing.
Posterior epistaxis, from the sphenopalatine artery behind the middle turbinate, occurs in older patients with hypertension, atherosclerosis or anticoagulation and can cause major blood loss and aspiration; it needs a posterior pack or balloon, then endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation or embolisation. Bleeding high in the nose after facial trauma may come from the anterior ethmoidal artery (an internal carotid branch via the ophthalmic artery), which is ligated through a medial orbital incision rather than embolised. Recurrent nosebleeds with mucocutaneous telangiectasia suggest hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia; unilateral bleeding with obstruction in an adolescent boy, juvenile angiofibroma.

title: Orbital cellulitis from ethmoid sinusitis
text:
The ethmoid air cells are separated from the orbit only by the paper-thin lamina papyracea, which has natural gaps for the ethmoidal vessels, and orbital veins are valveless. Ethmoid sinusitis in children therefore spreads easily into the orbit.
Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis involves only the eyelid tissues in front of the orbital septum: swollen red lids with a white eye and normal vision and eye movements, treated with oral antibiotics. Orbital (postseptal) cellulitis adds proptosis, painful or restricted eye movements, chemosis, reduced acuity or colour vision and a relative afferent pupillary defect. It is an emergency: contrast CT of the orbits and sinuses, IV antibiotics and joint ophthalmology and ENT care. A subperiosteal abscess along the medial wall or orbital abscess needs drainage. Untreated, it causes optic nerve compression and permanent blindness, and spread via the superior ophthalmic vein leads to cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis and brain abscess.

title: Frontal sinus: Pott puffy tumour and fractures
text:
The frontal sinuses develop from about age 6 and reach adult size after puberty; they drain via the frontonasal recess into the middle meatus. Frontal sinusitis in adolescents can cause osteomyelitis of the frontal bone with a subperiosteal abscess, a soft doughy swelling of the forehead (Pott puffy tumour). Infection spreads through the valveless diploic veins and the thin posterior table to cause epidural abscess, subdural empyema, meningitis or frontal lobe abscess, so every case needs contrast CT or MRI of the brain and combined surgical drainage.
Frontal sinus fractures follow high-energy blows to the forehead. Anterior table fractures cause a cosmetic depression; posterior table fractures breach the dura, causing CSF rhinorrhoea, pneumocephalus and meningitis; and injuries of the frontonasal outflow tract lead to later mucocele formation, which can erode into the orbit or cranium years afterward.

title: Nasolacrimal duct obstruction and dacryocystitis
text:
Tears drain through the puncta and canaliculi into the lacrimal sac at the medial canthus, then down the nasolacrimal duct to open under the inferior turbinate in the inferior meatus.
Congenital obstruction, from a persistent membrane at the lower end of the duct (valve of Hasner), affects about 1 in 20 infants: a watery eye with sticky discharge but a white eye. Most resolve by 12 months with lacrimal sac massage; persistent cases are probed. In adults, especially older women, acquired obstruction causes epiphora; infection of the stagnant sac (acute dacryocystitis) produces a tender red swelling BELOW the medial canthal tendon, with pus expressible from the puncta, and needs antibiotics and later a dacryocystorhinostomy, which opens the sac into the middle meatus of the nose.
Lacerations of the medial eyelid, including dog bites, often divide a canaliculus and need repair over a stent to prevent lifelong watering. Nasal packing or maxillary fractures can obstruct the duct.

title: Lacrimal gland: secretomotor pathway and dry eye
text:
Parasympathetic fibres for tear secretion start in the superior salivatory nucleus in the pons, travel in the nervus intermedius of the facial nerve to the geniculate ganglion, leave as the greater petrosal nerve, join the deep petrosal nerve to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal, synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion, and reach the lacrimal gland via the zygomatic and lacrimal nerves.
A facial nerve lesion at or proximal to the geniculate ganglion (for example a vestibular schwannoma, temporal bone fracture or Ramsay Hunt syndrome) reduces tear production and adds to the risk of exposure keratopathy; Schirmer testing measures it. After facial nerve regeneration, fibres meant for the salivary glands may sprout into the greater petrosal pathway, so the eye waters when the patient eats ('crocodile tears', gustatory lacrimation).
Other causes of dry eye include Sjögren syndrome, sarcoidosis and lymphoma infiltrating the gland. A lacrimal gland tumour (pleomorphic adenoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma, lymphoma) presents as a mass in the superotemporal orbit pushing the eye down and inward.

title: Giant cell arteritis and arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy
text:
Giant cell arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis of the extracranial branches of the carotid arteries and the aorta in people over 50, frequently with polymyalgia rheumatica. Features: new temporal headache, scalp tenderness (pain combing the hair), jaw claudication, a thickened, tender, pulseless superficial temporal artery, fever, weight loss and a very high ESR and CRP.
The dreaded complication is sudden painless visual loss from occlusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries (branches of the ophthalmic artery) that supply the optic nerve head: arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, with a pale, 'chalky white' swollen disc. Central retinal artery occlusion and ophthalmic artery occlusion also occur. Loss is usually permanent and the second eye can follow within days, so high-dose corticosteroids are started IMMEDIATELY on suspicion, before confirmation. Diagnosis is by temporal artery ultrasound (a 'halo' sign) or biopsy of a 1 to 2 cm segment within two weeks of starting steroids, remembering that skip lesions give false negatives. Late complications are aortic aneurysm and dissection.

title: Posterior vitreous detachment and retinal detachment
text:
With age the vitreous gel liquefies and separates from the retina (posterior vitreous detachment), causing a sudden shower of floaters and flashes of light (photopsia) as it tugs on the retina. Most are benign, but traction can tear the retina, especially at the periphery; fluid then passes through the tear and lifts the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium (rhegmatogenous retinal detachment). Risk factors are myopia, previous cataract surgery, trauma and a detachment in the other eye.
The patient notices a dark curtain or shadow spreading across the visual field from the periphery (the field defect is opposite to the detached area), then loss of central vision if the macula detaches. New floaters and flashes need same-day dilated fundus examination; a tear can be sealed by laser or cryotherapy. A detachment with the macula still attached is an emergency operated on within about a day, by vitrectomy with a gas bubble or a scleral buckle, because outcome depends on whether the macula is involved. Tractional detachments occur in proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

title: Blunt eye trauma: hyphaema and globe rupture
text:
Blunt trauma tears iris or ciliary body vessels, and blood settles in the anterior chamber as a hyphaema with a visible fluid level. Complications are rebleeding (most often in the first few days), raised intraocular pressure from blocked drainage (especially in sickle cell disease or trait, where sickled cells clog the trabecular meshwork), corneal blood staining and associated angle recession, which causes glaucoma years later. Management is rest with the head raised, a protective shield, topical steroid and cycloplegic, and pressure monitoring; aspirin and NSAIDs are avoided.
Severe blunt force can rupture the globe where the sclera is thinnest: at the limbus and just behind the insertions of the rectus muscles. Signs are markedly reduced vision, a soft eye, a peaked or teardrop pupil pointing to the rupture site, prolapsed uveal tissue, 360-degree haemorrhagic chemosis and a deep or shallow anterior chamber. Nothing is put into or pressed on the eye; a rigid shield, antiemetics, tetanus cover, CT of the orbits and urgent surgical repair follow.

title: Auricular haematoma, perichondritis and the ear skin
text:
The skin of the anterior auricle is tightly bound to the perichondrium, which carries the blood supply of the avascular elastic cartilage. A shearing blow (rugby, wrestling, boxing) raises a subperichondrial haematoma that separates cartilage from its supply; untreated, the cartilage necroses and fibrocartilage forms the crumpled 'cauliflower ear'. The haematoma must be drained within a few days and a pressure dressing or bolster sutures applied to prevent reaccumulation.
Piercings through the cartilage of the upper helix can cause perichondritis, commonly with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which requires anti-pseudomonal antibiotics and can deform the ear. Relapsing polychondritis inflames the cartilage bilaterally but spares the non-cartilaginous lobule. Vesicles in the concha and external canal with a facial palsy indicate Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster of the geniculate ganglion). The thin skin of the helix is a common site for basal and squamous cell carcinoma and for chondrodermatitis nodularis helicis in people who sleep on that side.

title: Referred otalgia
text:
The ear receives sensory fibres from five nerves: the auriculotemporal branch of the mandibular nerve (anterior auricle, external canal, outer tympanic membrane), the great auricular nerve (C2-C3, lower auricle and lobule), the lesser occipital nerve, the auricular branch of the vagus (Arnold nerve, posterior canal and concha; touching it with a speculum can provoke coughing or fainting) and the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (middle ear and inner tympanic membrane), with a small facial nerve contribution.
Pain arising anywhere else supplied by these nerves can be felt in the ear. Earache with a normal ear examination should prompt examination of the teeth and temporomandibular joint (V3), tonsils and posterior tongue (IX: tonsillitis, quinsy, post-tonsillectomy pain, tonsil and tongue-base cancer), larynx and hypopharynx (X: cancer of the supraglottis or piriform fossa), and the cervical spine (C2-C3). Persistent unilateral otalgia in a smoker or drinker, particularly with dysphagia or hoarseness, is a red flag for head and neck cancer.

title: Acute mastoiditis and its complications
text:
The mastoid air cells communicate with the middle ear through the aditus and antrum, so acute otitis media can spread into them. Acute mastoiditis, mainly in young children, causes fever, a red, tender, fluctuant swelling behind the ear, and an auricle pushed outward and forward (upward in older children, downward in infants), with a bulging tympanic membrane. Contrast CT is performed when complications are suspected; treatment is IV antibiotics, grommet insertion and cortical mastoidectomy for abscess or failure to improve.
Complications follow the anatomy: a subperiosteal abscess; a Bezold abscess tracking from the mastoid tip deep to sternocleidomastoid into the neck; sigmoid sinus thrombosis (sometimes with septic emboli and otitic hydrocephalus); meningitis and temporal lobe or cerebellar abscess through the thin tegmen or posterior wall; facial nerve palsy; labyrinthitis; and petrous apicitis (Gradenigo syndrome: otorrhoea, deep facial or retro-orbital pain from the trigeminal ganglion, and abducens nerve palsy).
In infants the mastoid process is undeveloped (it grows as sternocleidomastoid pulls on it, from about two years), so the facial nerve leaves the stylomastoid foramen just under the skin and is at risk from a standard postauricular incision.

title: Auditory tube dysfunction and glue ear
text:
The auditory (Eustachian) tube joins the middle ear to the nasopharynx; it is normally closed and opened by tensor veli palatini (and levator veli palatini) during swallowing and yawning, equalising pressure and draining secretions. In young children it is shorter, wider and more horizontal, which is why middle ear infections are so common, and large adenoids around its nasopharyngeal opening block it.
Persistent tube dysfunction lets negative pressure draw fluid into the middle ear: otitis media with effusion ('glue ear'), the commonest cause of hearing loss in children, affecting speech and schooling. A dull, retracted tympanic membrane with a flat tympanogram is typical. Most resolve; persistent bilateral cases with hearing loss have ventilation tubes (grommets), with adenoidectomy in some. Cleft palate and Down syndrome predispose to it.
A new UNILATERAL middle ear effusion in an adult requires endoscopic examination of the nasopharynx to exclude nasopharyngeal carcinoma blocking the tube. Barotrauma during flying or diving descent occurs when a blocked tube cannot equalise pressure.
